newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Nordics pin EU hopes on Blair's Britain.
newsitem.headline: Nordics pin EU hopes on Blair's Britain.

text.p: Hopes are running high in Denmark and Sweden, themselves wary of excessive European integration, that the new British government will become a close ally on key European Union issues.

Copenhagen and Stockholm, both with Social Democratic leaders, were quick to point out areas of common interest with London following this month's crushing election victory of Labour leader Tony Blair.
"It is clear that these governments have reason to welcome New Labour," one EU diplomat said.

Blair, who made an impressive EU debut at last Friday's summit in the Dutch coastal resort of Noordwijk, has pledged a new, constructive approach to the 15-nation bloc after 18 years of Conservative bashing of Brussels.

His government has said it will sign up to the EU's Social Chapter on worker rights and that it supports the Nordic initiative to write in a chapter on unemployment in the new EU treaty expected to be agreed in Amsterdam on June 16-17.
Further pleasing Scandinavian Social Democratic leaders, Britain has signalled it will back efforts to boost the environment, consumer rights and openness.
"I see more common ground between Denmark and the UK after the change of government," Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen told Reuters at the weekend.
"I expect that the unemployment question, the enlargement process and environmental issues will receive a more generous treatment," said Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson.
Like Britain, the two Nordics struggle with Euroscepticism at home, limiting their room to manoeuvre in EU affairs.

Blair has made clear he will not rush into moves to hand over more powers to Brussels, for example maintaining his predecessor's firm opposition to give the EU a defence role -- sharing the position of both Denmark and Sweden, if for different reasons.
All three countries look set to wait to join economic and monetary union (EMU), the bloc's most ambitious undertaking this decade, until after its planned 1999 start.

Britain has the possibility to opt out from the single currency, Denmark has already decided not to join and Sweden is expected to decide soon against early entry, even if Stockholm does not have a formal right to stay outside if it qualifies.

In addition, Copenhagen hopes for common ground with London on issues concerning home and justice affairs in the ongoing negotiations on a new EU treaty, an area which touches on sensitive issues of national sovereignty for both countries.
"I think it would be natural for us to work closely together on these points," Denmark's Petersen said.
After Danes rejected the Maastricht treaty in 1992, Denmark won the right to opt out from policing and citizenship arrangements, apart from EMU and joint defence.
Already with the British Conservative government, however, the Nordics often found themselves on the same side as Britain in for example promoting free trade and industry deregulation.
"The political drawback of having been in the same corner as (former British Prime Minister) John Major has been reduced dramatically," one EU diplomat said.
However, some also warn that the Euroscepticism in Denmark and Sweden could be further highlighted with the arrival of a more EU-friendly British government.

"They run the risk of being seen as the odd men out instead of Britain because they can't hide behind them anymore," one EU official said. "It is clear that they (Britain) have jumped over the two Nordic countries into centre stage."

"Denmark has in the past been able to hide itself behind British Euroscepticism to a certain degree, now we will have to sort out exactly where we stand on European issues," said Uffe Ellemann-Jensen, leader of Denmark's opposition Liberal party.
